facts.statement: Joined McNelly’s force in Texas in 1874, but George Durham disputed his status as a regular Ranger.

interpretation.note: Interpretation of the documented life and works; no claim of personal acquaintance from shared themes.

appraisal.note: AETERNUS editorial judgement; not presented as a historical quotation.

en.tagline: The border remembered by a newspaper man.
en.intro: Jennings carried a journalist’s sense of incident into his account of the Texas Rangers. A Texas Ranger is vigorous recollection, but the narrator’s exact position in the force has itself been contested.
en.orientation: The distinction matters. George Durham described him as a field clerk rather than a regular Ranger; the memoir’s claim to experience must be read with that disagreement in view.
origin: Born in Philadelphia, Jennings went to Texas as a young man. He later worked for newspapers in several American cities.
career: His association with McNelly’s force in the 1870s supplied material for a book published in 1899. Reporting and the retrospective shaping of adventure meet in its pages.
literature: The narrative offers a particular version of border service. Its energetic scenes are evidence of a memory being made public, as well as of the events remembered.
en.legacy: Jennings is worth reading as a participant in the making of Ranger legend. The question of his service sharpens the distinction between witness, narrator and public image.
en.bridge: The edition presents the complete account for readers who wish to examine the border story behind the legend.
